references.text: Isaiah's prophecy about Tyre and Sidon as pagan cities under God's judgment, which Jesus uses as a basis for comparison to show that Chorazin and Bethsaida are in a worse position.
Ezekiel's judgment against Sidon. Jesus refers to Tyre and Sidon as cities that were struck by God's judgment, yet would have repented if they had seen Jesus' miracles.
The people of Nineveh repented in sackcloth and ashes, which Jesus implies here that Tyre and Sidon also would have done if they had witnessed his mighty works.
Job sat in ashes as a sign of mourning and humility – the same symbolism Jesus uses regarding sackcloth and ashes as signs of repentance.
Daniel fasted in sackcloth and ashes as an expression of prayer and repentance, the same imagery Jesus uses here.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus pronounces the same woe over Chorazin and Bethsaida and compares them to Tyre and Sidon.
The continuation in Matthew where Jesus also pronounces woe upon Capernaum, which is further developed in Luke 10:15.
The immediate continuation in Luke where Jesus says it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment, and pronounces judgment against Capernaum.
Isaiah's prophecy about being cast down to Sheol, which Jesus uses in the next verse regarding Capernaum – the context underscores the seriousness of the woe pronounced over the Galilean cities.
Joel speaks of judgment against Tyre and Sidon. Jesus uses these cities as examples of pagan cities that would nevertheless have responded better to God's works than the Jewish cities did.
Bethsaida is mentioned as the place where Jesus performed miracles, making the woe pronounced over the city especially serious – they had seen his power but did not repent.
